scenes.narration: To understand where Ali Razmara ended up, start with where Ali Razmara began. Ali Razmara, also known as Haj Ali Razmara (Persian: علی رزم‌آرا, romanized: ali Razm-ārā; 30 March 1901 – 7 March 1951), was an Iranian military officer and politician who served as the prime minister of Iran from 1950 to 1951. He was assassinated by 26-year-old Khalil Tahmasebi of the Fada'iyan-e Islam organization outside the Shah Mosque in Tehran at the age of 49.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Ali Razmara ran through years nobody filmed. In January 1965, Hasan Ali Mansur became the fourth Iranian Prime Minister to be assassinated, also by a Fada'iyan-e Islam member. Razmara was born on 30 March 1901, on the night before Eid al-Adha, in Tehran.

Each stage of the life of Ali Razmara made the next stage possible. After returning to Iran, he was promoted to the rank of major while serving as a battalion commander. His performance as commander of the Kermanshah Regiment was so notable that in 1932, while retaining his existing position, he was also appointed acting commander of the Lorestan Brigade.

The people who knew Ali Razmara young describe someone already restless. When the French General François-Georges Gendre established the War College in Iran, Ali Razmara was appointed his deputy and became a professor there. In 1939, after nineteen years of military service, he attained the rank of Brigadier General and was appointed to the Supreme Military Council.

What Ali Razmara built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. However, he was never able to assume a higher position in the army. The reason was reportedly a case before the Military Prosecutor's Office accusing Razmara of failing to carry out the death sentence of a member of a tribal group.

By the time Ali Razmara reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. In September 1941, when Allied forces invaded Iran, he recommended a cessation of hostilities at a meeting of the Supreme War Council in the presence of Reza Shah. Following the collapse of the Iranian army, in October 1941 he was appointed commander of the 1st Division in Tehran and reorganized it.

The rise of Ali Razmara was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. In September 1941, following the Allied invasion and occupation of Iran during World War II, the Supreme War Council approved a plan to recruit contract soldiers, but Razmara refused to sign it. After Reza Shah's departure, his old associates also retired, creating opportunities for younger officers to advance.

Setbacks came early for Ali Razmara, and the response to them is the real story. Razmara was appointed commander of the 1st Central Division, replacing Major General Karim Buzarjomehri. In 1943, when the Allies arrested a large number of senior Iranian military figures on charges of fascist sympathies, Razmara was appointed Chief of the Army Staff.

The legacy of Ali Razmara outlived the circumstances that produced it. As his popularity increased, he was also given command of the Military Academy and responsibility for the Shah's Military Office. In 1944, Razmara was promoted to the rank of Major General and once again became Chief of the Joint Staff of the Imperial Iranian Army.

Few lives travel as far as that of Ali Razmara, and the distance is the point. His tenure as Army Chief coincided with the accidental exposure of several members of the Revenge Group, a secret organization formed to oppose individuals associated with foreign powers. Razmara's influence reportedly resulted in the suspects being released and prevented the names of the group's other members from becoming publicly known.

The childhood of Ali Razmara contains the adult in small print. According to Kamal Habibollahi, during Razmara's tenure as Chief of the Joint Staff, a serious effort was made to strengthen the Imperial Iranian Navy. This included beginning the dispatch of naval personnel to Britain for training and initiating efforts to establish complete Iranian naval control over the Persian Gulf without British presence.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Ali Razmara — in that order. When Ahmad Qavam came to power in 1946 amid serious political developments concerning Azerbaijan, Razmara was appointed Chief of the Army Staff. After the withdrawal of Red Army forces, while negotiations between the Azerbaijani Democratic Party and Qavam's government were still underway, the Shah ordered Razmara to prepare the army for an advance into Azerbaijan and Kurdistan.

The turning point in the life of Ali Razmara looked like a failure at the time. Although Qavam had been the most important figure in securing the withdrawal of Soviet forces from Azerbaijan in 1946 and preventing its annexation by the Soviet Union, he did not take decisive action against the Azerbaijani Democratic Party and the Republic of Mahabad. First, his government was allied with the Tudeh Party, which itself was an ally of Ja'far Pishevari, the leader of the Azerbaijani Democratic Party.

Every biography of Ali Razmara has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. Second, Qavam knew that resolving the Azerbaijan issue and calming the country's political atmosphere would lead to an alliance between the Shah and Qavam's opponents in parliament, ultimately resulting in his own downfall. His negotiations with Pishevari came to an end when the Shah and Razmara first conducted an aerial reconnaissance mission over Azerbaijan, piloted by the Shah himself, and then presented Qavam with a fait accompli, forcing him to cooperate with the military advance.

The education of Ali Razmara happened mostly outside any school. He later emphasized that he had opposed the operation and that the Shah and Razmara had forced him to undertake the military campaign. However, Ebrahim Hakimi and subsequently Abdolhossein Hazhir became prime minister instead, and the previous closeness between the Shah and the Army Chief disappeared.

What Ali Razmara wanted at the start and what Ali Razmara got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Nevertheless, the highly decorated lieutenant general had such a strong position among the military that dismissing him was considered equivalent to risking a coup similar to the one that had brought Reza Khan to power. In an apparent effort to regain his favor, in April 1948 the Shah awarded Razmara the rank of Lieutenant General.

The defining trait of Ali Razmara was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. His name was recorded in the history of the Iranian Army as the fourth person to receive this rank. He promoted a plan for decentralization of government together with decentralization of the seven-year plan for infrastructure development and improvement.

Those who met Ali Razmara at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. His plan called for setting up local councils in Iran's 84 districts to run local affairs such as health, education and agricultural programs. One of his most enduring achievements was the institution of the Point IV program via agreement with US President Harry S.

The private years of Ali Razmara explain the public decades better than any speech. Razmara began trimming the government payrolls, eliminating a large number of officials out of a total of 187,000 civil servants. By so doing, Razmarra earned the wrath of the powerful land-owning and merchant families and most conservatives without gaining the confidence of the radical Tudeh Party.

The family Ali Razmara came from matters more than the legends admit. Additionally, his opposition to the expropriation of AIOC assets at Abadan earned him the wrath of the small but powerful group of Majlis deputies known as the National Front. The National Front was led by Majlis Member, Mohammad Mosaddegh, whose leading ally in Parliament was the Assembly Speaker, Ayatollah Kashani.

The first real success of Ali Razmara arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. Ali Razmara came closer than any other prime minister to ratifying the supplemental oil agreement between Iran and the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company (AIOC). The AIOC did, however, offer a few improvements: it guaranteed that its annual royalty payments would not drop below 4 million pounds; it would reduce the area where it would be allowed to drill; and it promised to train more Iranians for administrative jobs.

The last chapter of Ali Razmara was written long after the fame. Razmara asked Anglo-Iranian to revise some of the agreement terms, namely to allow Iranian auditors to review their financial activities, offer Iranians managerial jobs, and pay some of the royalties to the Iranian government in advance. Razmara was in office at the direct urging of the British Foreign Office and the AIOC to the Shah.

The whole life of Ali Razmara reads like a single decision repeated. On 7 March 1951, Razmara went to the Shah Mosque for a memorial service. The assassin, in the crowd, fired three quick shots, fatally wounding the Prime Minister.

Between the birth and the legend of Ali Razmara lie the years that actually decide it. Khalil Tahmasebi, a member of the group Fada'iyan-e Islam, was arrested at the scene. At a public demonstration the following day attended by more than 8,000 Tudeh Party members and National Front supporters, Fadayan-e Islam distributed leaflets carrying a threat to assassinate the Shah and other government officials if the assassin, Tahmasebi, was not set free immediately.

The reputation of Ali Razmara was built in the middle, not at the edges. Threats were also issued against any Majlis member who opposed oil nationalization. The National Front was led by Mohammad Mosaddegh, who became prime minister within two months of Razmara's assassination.

Somebody like Ali Razmara should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. Ayatollah Seyyed Abol-Ghasem Kashani ended his support for the Fadayan-e Islam after the assassination. On the other hand, the assassin, Tahmassebi, was freed by the Iranian Parliament in 1952, but following the 1953 Iranian coup d'état, Tahmasebi was re-arrested, tried and executed in 1955.

The life of Ali Razmara begins far from where the story usually starts. In 1954 Navvab Safavi, founder of the Fadayan-e Islam, in a speech to the Muslim Brotherhood meeting in Egypt, declared that he himself had killed Razmara. Razmara married Anvar ol Molouk Hedayat who was a sister of Sadegh Hedayat, an Iranian author.

Ali Razmara was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. One of his sons, Nowzar, was the SAVAK’s chief of station in Cairo, Egypt, in the late 1970s.
